newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dollar falls as markets test central bank.
newsitem.headline: Canada dollar falls as markets test central bank.

text.p: An unnerving cat and mouse game between Canada's central bank and currency market traders determined to test interest rate policy threatens to push the Canadian dollar to a two-year low, economists said on Tuesday.
The Canadian dollar, currently trading at 71.79 U.S. cents, has edged down since June 26, when the Bank of Canada last raised interest rates in a fleeting effort to shore up the currency.
The latest weakness in the Canadian dollar has taken the currency to near 71.42 U.S. cents - its lowest level in two years.

Speculative selling in the past two months has winded the currency, and analysts fear a continued selloff could prompt a loosening of domestic monetary conditions -- a move that would conflict with the Bank of Canada's objective of a less stimulative monetary policy.

The central bank uses the so-called monetary conditions index (MCI), calculated from the market rate of 90-day commercial paper and the trade weighted-value of the Canadian dollar, to help chart monetary policy.

"The game that was initiated back in June was to test the Bank of Canada on the MCI (monetary conditions index) for sensitive levels in the currency," said Andrew Pyle, economist with ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Toronto.
"That same game is being played right now where the market feels that if it pushes the Canada dollar to 71.42 U.S. cents, it will get another rate hike," he said.
But the Bank of Canada seems content to let the dollar strengthen on the back of Canada's economic fundamentals rather than to trying to stimulate the currency through an interest rate hike.

"Canada's strong underlying economic fundamentals continue to support the currency market expectations that the Canadian dollar will appreciate over time," the central bank said in its summer review released on Tuesday.
But economists reckon that solid economic growth is not enough to curtail the expectation of an interest rate hike.
"Regardless of what the fundamentals are saying, the players out there are bent on testing the bank's resolve to hold the line," said Mario Angastiniotis, economist with MMS International in Toronto.
Analysts are split on whether the central bank will yield to market pressures or stand its ground and allow the currency to swoon to the 71.42 U.S. cent level.
"I don't think the bank will resort to a rate hike right away. In fact, I think foreign exchange intervention will be first. The rate hike is the last resort," Angastiniotis said.
Pyle, however, predicted an imminent rate hike.
"I wouldn't have been surprised to see the bank in this morning and we could easily see them in before the week's end," he said.
If the Canadian dollar weakens past 71.58 U.S. cents -- its low point just before the last rate hike -- the bank would move again to raise rates, Pyle said.
Internal political problems remain the wild card for the Canadian dollar.

Economists said that a recent war of words between Canadian government leaders and Quebec's separatist Premier Lucien Bouchard could refocus market fears of a renewed constitutional rumble when parliament reconvenes in the fall.

"For now, it's just noise in the background. Where it becomes a real undermining factor for the currency is when parliament reconvenes and we get closer to 1998 and another Quebec election," Pyle said.
